guide.title: About JPG compression
guide.markdown:
### What is JPG compression?

A JPG is compressed the moment it is saved. JPEG, named after the Joint Photographic Experts Group that started work on it in 1986, cuts a picture into 8x8 pixel blocks. Each block is turned into a set of frequencies with a discrete cosine transform, the finest frequencies are rounded off, and what is left is packed with Huffman coding. That rounding saves the space, and the quality number says how coarse it gets.

So compressing a JPG means saving it again with coarser rounding. Cameras and phones often store photos at a high quality, keeping detail that a web page, a chat message or an email never shows. Decoding such a file and encoding it at a lower quality gives a lighter file with the same width and height. Typical JPEG settings already shrink a picture to a tenth or a twentieth of its raw size, so a second pass saves most on files that were saved generously.

Three things decide how heavy a JPG is: how many pixels it has, how much fine detail and noise it holds, and how much metadata rides along. A 12-megapixel photo of grass is heavy at any quality. A small, smooth graphic stays light.

### Programs that compress JPG files

**Windows**

- Adobe Photoshop: Export As has a Quality setting for JPG.
- GIMP: free editor whose JPEG export dialog has a Quality slider.

**Mac**

- Preview: Export shows a Quality slider when JPEG is picked.
- Photos: exports photos as JPEG with a quality and a size choice.

**Linux**

- GIMP: the same JPEG export as on Windows and Mac.
- ImageMagick: `magick photo.jpg -quality 80 smaller.jpg` re-encodes from a terminal, on any system.
- jpegtran: rewrites a JPG without decoding it to pixels, for example with `-optimize` or `-progressive`, so the picture stays exactly the same and the saving is small.

**Web**

- This page: MozJPEG at quality 82, run by your browser.

**Mobile**

- iPhone: Preview in iOS 26 exports JPEG with a Size slider.
- Any phone: this page works in a mobile browser.

### Original and compressed JPG compared

- **Format**: both are JPEG files, image/jpeg, ending in .jpg. Any program that opened the original opens the copy.
- **Pixels**: the width and height are the same. Nothing is cropped or scaled.
- **Encoder and quality**: the copy is written by MozJPEG, an encoder tuned to get more out of the JPEG format, at quality 82. Quality numbers aren't a shared scale, so 82 here and 82 in another program can look different.
- **Layout**: the copy is a progressive JPEG with optimized Huffman tables. A progressive file shows a coarse picture early and fills in detail as it loads.
- **Metadata**: the copy carries no EXIF, ICC profile or XMP. Camera settings, the date taken and GPS location stay only in your original.
- **Size**: usually smaller. If it isn't, you get the original back, so a download is never larger than what you chose.

Every JPEG save is lossy, including this one. Compress from the best copy you have, once, rather than squeezing the same file again and again.

### Other ways to compress a JPG

- **Preview (Mac)**: open the image, choose File > Export, pick JPEG, drag the Quality slider down and click Save.
- **Photos (Mac)**: select the photos, choose File > Export > Export Photos, set Photo Kind to JPEG, then lower JPEG Quality or pick a smaller Size.
- **Preview (iPhone, iOS 26)**: open the file, tap the actions button next to its name, tap Export, choose JPEG and drag the Size slider. The slider applies to JPEG and HEIC exports.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: choose File > Export As, give the file a .jpg name, then lower Quality in the export dialog, which starts at 85. Each export compresses the picture again.
- **Adobe Photoshop (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Export > Export As, pick JPG, lower the Quality setting and click Export.

### Problems with compressing JPG files

- **The same file came back**: the quality 82 encode wasn't smaller, which happens with JPGs that were already saved light. Reduce the pixel size instead.
- **Still over an upload limit**: scale the photo down first, for example with Tools > Adjust Size in Preview or Image > Scale Image in GIMP, then compress the smaller copy.
- **Sharp text and lines turn fuzzy**: JPEG blurs hard edges. Keep screenshots, logos and diagrams as PNG and shrink them with the [PNG compressor](/compress-png/).
- **The location and camera details are gone**: the copy has no EXIF. Keep your original when you need them.
- **Colors look a little flat**: the ICC profile isn't copied, so a photo tagged with a wide-gamut profile such as Display P3 is shown as plain sRGB.
- **Blocks appear after several rounds**: each pass loses detail. Go back to the original rather than compressing a compressed copy.

guide.title: About JPEG compression
guide.markdown:
### What is JPEG compression?

JPEG is a lossy way of storing photos, first published as ITU-T T.81 in 1992 and as ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994. It is built into most digital cameras and scanners, and every major browser shows it. Its trick is to keep what the eye notices and drop what it doesn't. Brightness is kept in more detail than color, small blocks of the picture are turned into frequency patterns, and the subtle patterns are stored with less precision or not at all.

The quality number controls that precision through tables of rounding steps. A high quality keeps almost everything and makes a big file. A lower one rounds harder, and the file shrinks. The scale usually runs from 0 to 100, but each program maps it to its own tables, which is why the same number gives different files in different apps.

Some arithmetic shows why the setting matters. A 12-megapixel photo is 12 million pixels with three color values each, about 36 MB before compression. At typical settings, a tenth to a twentieth of that, it lands somewhere between 1.8 and 3.6 MB, and a lower quality pushes it further down.

Compressing a JPEG that already exists means decoding it to pixels and encoding those pixels again with harder rounding. There is also a lossless kind of tidying: rewriting the file's coding tables or switching it to progressive order without touching the picture. That saves far less, but nothing is lost.

### Programs that compress JPEG files

**Windows**

- Adobe Photoshop: the Quality setting in Export As decides the JPEG's size.
- GIMP: with Show preview in image window ticked, its JPEG export dialog shows the file size each quality gives.

**Mac**

- Preview: re-exports a JPEG with a Least-to-Best Quality slider.
- Photos: can export a batch of photos as smaller JPEGs.

**Linux**

- GIMP: free on every desktop system.
- MozJPEG's cjpeg: the command-line version of the encoder this page uses.

**Web**

- Squoosh: a web app from Google Chrome Labs that shows the original and the compressed version side by side.
- This page: MozJPEG at a fixed quality of 82, with several files at once.

**Mobile**

- iPhone: Preview in iOS 26 has a Size slider when exporting a JPEG.
- Android and other phones: use this page in the browser.

### Lossy and lossless JPEG compression compared

- **Re-encoding (what this page does)**: the picture is decoded and saved again at quality 82. Savings are large on photos saved at a high quality, and a little detail is lost.
- **Lossless optimizing**: tools such as jpegtran rewrite the existing data with better coding tables or in progressive order. The pixels stay identical, and the file usually shrinks only a little.
- **Progressive and baseline**: a baseline JPEG loads top to bottom, while a progressive one appears blurry first and sharpens. This page writes progressive JPEGs.
- **Metadata**: thumbnails, EXIF, XMP and color profiles can add a noticeable amount to a small file. Re-encoding here leaves them out.
- **Pixel size**: neither kind of compression changes the width and height. Scaling down is a separate step, and the one that cuts size the most.
- **What stays the same**: the result is still image/jpeg, with 8 bits per color channel and no transparency or layers.

### Other ways to compress a JPEG

- **Preview (Mac)**: choose File > Export, set the format to JPEG, drag Quality down, then click Save.
- **Photos (Mac)**: choose File > Export > Export Photos, set Photo Kind to JPEG and lower JPEG Quality or Size.
- **Preview (iPhone, iOS 26)**: tap the actions button beside the file name, tap Export, pick JPEG and move the Size slider, which works for JPEG and HEIC.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: choose File > Export As with a .jpg or .jpeg name and lower Quality from its default of 85. Every export re-compresses.
- **Adobe Photoshop (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Export > Export As, select JPG and drag Quality down before clicking Export.

### Problems with JPEG compression

- **A form rejects .jpeg but takes .jpg**: the format is the same. Rename the ending, or convert with the [JPEG to JPG converter](/jpeg-to-jpg/).
- **The file is still too large after compressing**: its pixel dimensions are the main cost. Resize it, then compress again.
- **Smooth skies show bands or blocks**: gradients suffer most when a JPEG is squeezed. Start from a higher-quality original.
- **A logo lost its transparent background**: JPEG has no alpha channel. Keep such images as PNG or WebP, and shrink a WebP with the [WebP compressor](/compress-webp/).
- **The compressor returned the file unchanged**: the new encode wasn't smaller. The JPEG is already lean at this quality.

guide.title: About MOV files
guide.markdown:
### What is a MOV file?

MOV is the QuickTime File Format. Apple introduced it with QuickTime in 1991 and brought QuickTime to Windows in 1994. Files end in .mov, or occasionally .qt, and are labeled video/quicktime. A MOV is a container: it holds separate tracks for video, sound, text and timecode, packed in building blocks called atoms. Software skips atoms it doesn't recognize, which let the format grow over the years without breaking older players.

The tracks inside can use many codecs. Common ones are H.264 or HEVC for everyday video, Apple ProRes and Motion JPEG for editing, and AAC or uncompressed PCM for sound. That range is why two MOV files can behave very differently: one plays everywhere, another needs special software.

You meet MOV files on Apple devices. The iPhone camera records them, a Mac saves screen recordings as MOV, and editing apps such as Final Cut Pro export them. They arrive by AirDrop, in cloud folders and as email attachments. Outside Apple's world they cause trouble, because browser support for MOV is limited, and Apple itself now generally uses MP4 for sharing.

### Programs that open MOV files

**Windows**

- VLC: plays most MOV files with its own codecs.
- Microsoft Clipchamp: imports a MOV and exports it as MP4.
- Adobe Premiere Pro: edits MOV footage, ProRes included.

**Mac**

- QuickTime Player: Apple's built-in player and the format's home.
- Final Cut Pro: Apple's editor, which reads and writes MOV.
- VLC: a fallback for unusual codecs.

**Linux**

- VLC and mpv: free players that read MOV.
- FFmpeg: converts or inspects MOV files from the terminal.

**Web**

- Safari plays MOV. Other browsers are inconsistent, which is the usual reason to convert.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: MOV is the camera's own format, so Photos and Files play it.
- Android: VLC for Android plays most MOV files.

### MOV and MP4 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .mov or .qt with video/quicktime; .mp4 or .m4v with video/mp4.
- **Origins**: MOV is Apple's own format. MP4 is MPEG-4 Part 14, ISO/IEC 14496-14, published in 2003. Its structure, the ISO Base Media File Format, was derived from QuickTime, so MOV's atoms and MP4's boxes are the same idea, yet the two formats aren't interchangeable.
- **Typical codecs**: MOV is a common home for editing codecs such as ProRes. MP4 is the usual home of delivery codecs: H.264 video with AAC sound, and also HEVC, AV1, VP9, MP3 or Opus.
- **Playback**: every major browser plays MP4. MOV plays reliably only in Apple software and in players like VLC.
- **File size**: the container hardly matters. The codec and bitrate decide size, so the same H.264 video takes the same room as MOV or MP4.

What this page writes: H.264 video with x264's ultrafast preset at CRF 32, AAC sound at 96 kbps, the picture capped at 1920 px on its longer side and 30 frames a second, interlaced footage deinterlaced, and the index moved to the front of the file so playback can start before it has fully loaded.

### Other ways to convert MOV to MP4

- **VLC (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: choose Media > Convert/Save, click Add and pick the MOV, choose an MP4 profile from the Profile menu, set the Destination file and click Start. VLC's guide doesn't list its profiles by name.
- **FFmpeg (command line)**: `ffmpeg -i input.mov -c copy output.mp4` moves the tracks into an MP4 without re-encoding, so nothing is lost. It fails when the MOV holds a codec MP4 can't carry; leave out `-c copy` to re-encode instead.
- **Microsoft Clipchamp (Windows, web)**: add the MOV to a Clipchamp project, use the Export button in the top-right corner and pick a resolution. The video is re-encoded and saved as MP4.

### Problems with MOV files

- **It won't play in Chrome, Firefox or a Windows app**: convert it to MP4 here, or open it in VLC.
- **An iPhone video shows sound but no picture on Windows**: the video is probably HEVC, which Windows needs Microsoft's HEVC Video Extensions to play. The H.264 MP4 made here doesn't.
- **A website or form refuses the upload**: many accept MP4 but not MOV. Upload the converted file.
- **The MP4 looks softer than the MOV**: this page favors speed and size. Keep the MOV as your master copy.
- **It takes a long time**: a big MOV is decoded and encoded on your own device. Plug a laptop in and leave the tab open.
- **"FFmpeg failed with exit code N"**: the MOV couldn't be decoded, which usually means a damaged or half-copied file. Copy or download it again.
- **You need a GIF or just the sound**: use the [MOV to GIF converter](/mov-to-gif/) or the [MOV to MP3 converter](/mov-to-mp3/).

guide.title: About SVG files
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

SVG, Scalable Vector Graphics, is an open standard from the W3C. SVG 1.0 became a Recommendation in 2001 and SVG 1.1 in 2003. An SVG file is XML text that describes a two-dimensional drawing as shapes, paths, text and embedded images. Because it stores drawing instructions rather than pixels, it can be drawn at any size and stay sharp.

Being text has side effects. An SVG can be opened in a text editor, searched, indexed and compressed; a gzip-compressed copy uses the .svgz ending. It works with CSS and JavaScript, so it can be styled, animated and scripted, and it supports clipping paths, masks and filter effects. An SVG can stand alone as a file or sit inside an HTML page.

You meet SVG files as logos, icons, charts and diagrams. Design tools such as Figma, Illustrator and Inkscape export them, icon libraries ship them, and many websites draw their logos with them. The catch is that many apps and upload forms accept only raster images, and some refuse SVG because it can carry scripts.

### Programs that open SVG files

**Windows**

- Inkscape: free vector editor that uses SVG as its own format.
- Adobe Illustrator: opens and exports SVG.
- Microsoft Edge and other browsers: show the drawing when you open the file.

**Mac**

- Inkscape and Illustrator: the same editing as on Windows.
- Safari, Chrome and Firefox: display SVG files you drag in.

**Linux**

- Inkscape: the usual choice for editing.
- rsvg-convert: the librsvg command-line tool, which renders SVG to PNG.
- GIMP: opens an SVG as a pixel image at a size you pick.

**Web**

- Every major browser displays SVG, and Figma imports it.

**Mobile**

- Phone browsers show SVG files and web pages that use them.

**Any system**

- A text editor shows the SVG's XML, which you can edit by hand.

### SVG and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .svg or .svgz with image/svg+xml; .png with image/png.
- **How the picture is stored**: SVG keeps shapes and text as instructions. PNG keeps a fixed grid of pixels, compressed losslessly with DEFLATE.
- **Scaling**: an SVG redraws cleanly at any size. A PNG blurs or turns blocky when enlarged past its pixels.
- **File size**: a simple icon is tiny as SVG. A complex illustration can be larger as SVG than as PNG, and a PNG grows with its pixel count.
- **Transparency**: both have it. An SVG is clear wherever nothing is drawn; a PNG stores an alpha value for every pixel.
- **Text**: in an SVG it stays real text. In a PNG it becomes pixels.
- **Motion**: SVG can animate. This page writes a single still PNG.
- **Color depth**: PNG allows 1 to 16 bits per sample; the PNG written here has 8 bits per channel.

How this page draws it: your browser renders the SVG at the size it reports, one SVG unit to one pixel, onto a transparent canvas, and the canvas is saved as a PNG. There is no scale setting.

### Other ways to convert SVG to PNG

- **Inkscape (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: open the SVG, choose File > Export PNG Image (Shift+Ctrl+E), pick Page, Drawing or Selection, set the size and export. The background is transparent unless you give it an opacity in Document Properties.
- **Adobe Illustrator (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Export > Export As, pick PNG and click Export, then set the resolution and background color, which can be transparent, white or black.

guide.title: About JFIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JFIF file?

JFIF stands for JPEG File Interchange Format. The JPEG standard says how to compress a photo but leaves out details that programs need to swap files reliably, such as the color model and the pixel shape. JFIF fills that gap with a minimal wrapper, which is why most files people call JPEGs are really JFIF files.

The wrapper is small. A JFIF file opens with JPEG's start-of-image marker, followed at once by an APP0 segment labeled JFIF. That segment gives a version number, the resolution in dots per inch or per centimeter, and room for an optional small thumbnail. The compressed picture follows. Eric Hamilton of C-Cube Microsystems wrote the first versions, with 1.02 dating from 1992, and the format was later standardized as ITU-T T.871 and ISO/IEC 10918-5.

JFIF files may end in .jfif, .jfi, .jif, .jpe, .jpeg or .jpg, and all of them are image/jpeg. You see the .jfif ending mostly on Windows, where some PCs save pictures downloaded from a browser that way. The file is fine; the ending is what trips up other apps and upload forms.

### Programs that open JFIF files

**Windows**

- Photos: opens .jfif files as ordinary pictures.
- Paint: opens .jfif pictures for quick edits.
- Browsers: show a .jfif dragged into a tab.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens the file and exports a JPEG copy.
- Adobe Photoshop: opens the file and exports a JPG.

**Linux**

- GIMP: opens the JPEG data inside and exports a .jpg.
- ImageMagick: `magick photo.jfif photo.jpg` writes a re-encoded JPG copy.

**Web**

- Every major browser shows JFIF files, since they are served as image/jpeg.

**Mobile**

- Phone browsers display a .jfif image from a web page like any JPEG.

### JFIF and JPG compared

- **Image data**: the same JPEG compression, with 8x8 blocks, a discrete cosine transform and Huffman coding.
- **Extensions and media type**: .jfif is one of several JFIF endings, next to .jpg and .jpeg. All share image/jpeg.
- **Header**: a JFIF file starts with an APP0 segment. Many camera JPGs carry an Exif segment instead, or as well, with shooting details.
- **Extras**: JFIF can hold a tiny thumbnail and a resolution; Exif adds camera settings, dates and location.
- **Color**: 8 bits per channel and no transparency, in both.
- **What this page does**: decodes the picture, then writes a fresh JPEG at quality 0.85 from its pixels, without the thumbnail, EXIF, ICC profile or XMP.

Renaming is the lossless option: change .jfif to .jpg and every byte stays the same. Convert instead when you want a fresh file or many files at once without renaming each.

### Other ways to convert JFIF to JPG

- **Rename on Windows**: in File Explorer, turn on endings with View > Show > File name extensions in Windows 11, or the File name extensions box on the View tab in Windows 10. Then rename the file and replace .jfif with .jpg.
- **Rename on a Mac**: select the file, open Get Info, and change the ending in Name & Extension. To see endings everywhere, turn on Show all filename extensions in Finder > Settings > Advanced.
- **Preview (Mac)**: open the file, choose File > Export, pick JPEG from the Format pop-up menu and click Save. A JFIF is already JPEG data, so exporting compresses it again.
- **Adobe Photoshop (Windows, Mac)**: open the .jfif, then use File > Export > Export As with JPG as the format and click Export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: open the .jfif, choose File > Export As, change the ending of the name to .jpg and click Export.

### Problems with JFIF files

- **An upload form says the type isn't allowed**: it checks the ending. Convert the file here or rename it to .jpg.
- **Saved images keep arriving as .jfif**: some Windows PCs choose that ending for JPEG downloads. Rename them after saving, or convert a batch here.
- **An app won't open the file**: it may not know the .jfif ending. Rename it to .jpg and try again.
- **You can't see a .jfif ending at all**: Windows and macOS hide many endings by default. Turn them on as described above, or check the file's type in its properties or Get Info window.
- **You need transparency or lossless edits**: JPEG has neither. Use the [JFIF to PNG converter](/jfif-to-png/).

guide.title: About video to GIF
guide.markdown:
### What is a video file?

A video file is a container with tracks inside. The container, such as MP4, MOV, WebM or AVI, decides how the tracks are packed and labeled. The codecs inside decide how the picture and sound are squeezed: H.264, HEVC, VP9 or AV1 for the picture, and AAC, MP3 or Opus for the sound. That is why two .mp4 files can play differently on the same device.

The picture track is a run of still frames, usually 24, 30 or 60 a second. Video codecs save space by storing most frames as changes from the ones before, so a long clip can still be small. A GIF has no such trick. Each frame is a separate picture, so turning video into GIF is really choosing which stills to keep and how to color them.

This page takes MP4, the most common video format, from phones, cameras, screen recorders and editors. Other containers have their own pages: [MOV to GIF](/mov-to-gif/), [WebM to GIF](/webm-to-gif/) and [AVI to GIF](/avi-to-gif/).

### Programs that play and trim video files

**Windows**

- Media Player: the built-in player for MP4 and most common video.
- Microsoft Clipchamp: trims clips and can export short ones as GIF.
- VLC: plays nearly any video, with its own codecs.

**Mac**

- QuickTime Player: plays MP4 and MOV, and Edit > Trim cuts a clip down.
- iMovie: Apple's free editor for longer edits.

**Linux**

- VLC and mpv: free players.
- FFmpeg: cuts, scales and converts from the terminal.

**Web**

- Browsers: MP4 with H.264 plays in all the major ones.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: the Photos app trims a video in its editor.
- Android: Google Photos and most gallery apps can trim a clip before you share it.

### Video and GIF compared

- **Frames**: video often runs at 30 or 60 frames a second. This page keeps 15, so a 4-second clip becomes 60 images in the GIF.
- **Size of the picture**: the GIF is at most 480 px on its longer side, with both sides rounded down to an even number. A 1920x1080 clip comes out at 480x270.
- **Color**: a video frame can use millions of colors. A GIF image uses a palette of at most 256, so this page reads the whole clip first, builds one palette that suits it, then maps every frame onto that palette.
- **Compression**: video stores differences between frames. GIF stores each frame with LZW, which is lossless, but it can't predict motion, so a GIF is usually much larger than a video of the same length and size.
- **Sound**: video can carry it; GIF can't.
- **Playback**: a GIF starts by itself and needs no player, which is why chat apps, forums and email accept it where they block video. The GIF made here loops forever.
- **Media types**: video/mp4 for MP4; image/gif for GIF, a format CompuServe introduced in 1987.

### Other ways to convert video to GIF

- **Adobe Photoshop (Windows, Mac)**: import the clip with File > Import > Video Frames to Layers, turn the layers into a frame animation in Window > Timeline, then export with File > Export > Save for Web (Legacy) and choose GIF. Photoshop reads MP4, MOV, AVI and MPEG when the right codecs are installed, and may not import a long video in full.
- **Microsoft Clipchamp (Windows, web)**: put the clip on a project timeline, press Export in the top-right corner and pick GIF. Clipchamp offers GIF only for videos up to 15 seconds long.
- **FFmpeg (command line)**: `ffmpeg -i input.mp4 output.gif` works, but its palette is a general-purpose one that isn't tuned to the clip. For truer color, make a palette from the clip first with the palettegen filter and apply it with paletteuse, the method this page uses. Frame timing in a GIF counts in hundredths of a second, so no delay can be shorter than 0.01 s.

### Problems with video to GIF

- **The page won't take your file**: it accepts MP4 only. Use the converter for your video's format.
- **The GIF is too heavy to post**: shorten the clip before converting. Every second adds 15 frames, so the file grows with the length.
- **Small text is unreadable**: the 480 px limit shrinks screen recordings a lot. Crop to the part that matters, or share the video instead.
- **Shading turns into dots or steps**: 256 colors per frame can't hold a smooth gradient. Clips with flat colors convert best.
- **It takes a long time**: FFmpeg runs on your device in a single thread. Keep the tab open, and on a laptop plug in.
- **"FFmpeg failed with exit code N"**: the video couldn't be read. Make sure it plays in your usual player; if it doesn't, the file is probably damaged or incomplete.
- **You wanted the audio**: a GIF has none. The [MP4 to MP3 converter](/mp4-to-mp3/) saves the sound instead.

guide.title: About M4A files
guide.markdown:
### What is an M4A file?

M4A is the ending for MPEG-4 files that carry sound and no picture. The container is the same one MP4 video uses; the A just tells software to expect audio. Apple adopted the ending for unprotected music, and its media type is audio/mp4.

Inside, most M4A files hold AAC, the Advanced Audio Coding defined in MPEG-4 Part 3. AAC was designed to sound better than MP3 at the same bitrate, and it handles sample rates from 8 to 96 kHz and bitrates up to 512 kbps. Some M4A files hold Apple Lossless instead, which keeps the sound exactly but is much larger.

You meet M4A files in several places. Songs sold through iTunes used AAC. The iPhone's Voice Memos app saves its recordings as M4A, and audio ripped or imported with Apple's apps often ends up in the format too. Protected purchases use a sister ending, .m4p, and can't be played outside Apple's own software.

### Programs that open M4A files

**Windows**

- Media Player: Windows 11's built-in player handles M4A.
- iTunes: plays M4A and can make MP3 copies.
- VLC: plays it with its own decoders.

**Mac**

- Music: Apple's player and library, which can convert songs to MP3.
- QuickTime Player: plays a single file.

**Linux**

- VLC: plays M4A out of the box.
- Audacity: imports M4A for editing once its FFmpeg library is installed.

**Web**

- Every major browser plays AAC in an MP4 container, so an M4A plays when dragged into a tab.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: Music, Files and Voice Memos.
- Android: plays AAC in .m4a files on every version.

### M4A and MP3 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .m4a with audio/mp4; .mp3 with audio/mpeg.
- **Codec**: M4A usually holds AAC and sometimes Apple Lossless. MP3 is one codec, MPEG-1 Audio Layer III, standardized as ISO/IEC 11172-3 in 1993 and extended by ISO/IEC 13818-3 in 1995.
- **Compression**: both AAC and MP3 are lossy and rely on a model of hearing to drop sounds listeners are unlikely to notice. AAC does more with fewer bits.
- **Range**: MP3 runs from 32 to 320 kbps at 32, 44.1 or 48 kHz. At 128 kbps an MP3 is about an eleventh the size of the same music on a CD.
- **Tags**: an M4A keeps titles and artwork in MPEG-4 metadata; an MP3 keeps them in ID3 blocks. This page leaves out cover art and doesn't promise that other tags come across, so check them after converting.
- **Support**: MP3 plays almost everywhere, from browsers to old car stereos. M4A plays in browsers and on phones but trips up some older hardware and software.
- **History**: MP3 was developed at Fraunhofer IIS from the late 1980s with partners in the MPEG audio group. Its patent licensing program ended on 23 April 2017.

What this page writes: an MP3 encoded with LAME at a constant 192 kbps. A minute of audio comes to about 1.4 MB, whatever the bitrate of the M4A you start from.

### Other ways to convert M4A to MP3

- **Apple Music (Mac)**: in Music > Settings > Files > Import Settings, set Import Using to MP3 Encoder, select the songs, then choose File > Convert > Create MP3 Version. Protected purchases can't be converted, and going from one lossy format to another costs some quality.
- **iTunes (Windows)**: choose Edit > Preferences, click General, then Import Settings, and set Import Using to MP3 Encoder. Select the songs and choose File > Convert > Create MP3 Version. Store purchases convert only if they are iTunes Plus songs.
- **VLC (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: open Media > Convert/Save, add the M4A with the Add button, pick an MP3 audio profile under Profile, choose where to save it as the Destination file, then press Start.
- **FFmpeg (command line)**: `ffmpeg -i input.m4a -c:a libmp3lame output.mp3`. MP3 encoding needs an FFmpeg build that includes the LAME library.

### Problems with M4A files

- **A car stereo or old player ignores the file**: it may not know AAC in MP4. An MP3 copy plays on nearly everything.
- **The file ends in .m4p**: it may be copy-protected, and a protected file can't be converted. An unprotected one converts with the [M4P to MP3 converter](/m4p-to-mp3/).
- **The MP3 is larger than the M4A**: the original used a low bitrate, which is common for voice recordings. That is normal, since this page always writes 192 kbps.
- **The artwork is missing**: cover art isn't carried into the MP3. Add it back in your player, for example with Get Info in Apple Music.
- **"FFmpeg failed with exit code N"**: the audio couldn't be decoded, perhaps because the file is cut short or isn't really an M4A. Play it first to check.
- **You plan to edit the audio**: every lossy save costs a little. The [M4A to WAV converter](/m4a-to-wav/) makes an uncompressed copy to work on, with no second lossy step.

guide.title: About AVIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is an AVIF file?

Most AVIF files people want to convert were saved from a web page. Image services and content delivery networks send AVIF to browsers that support it because the files are small, so a picture that looked ordinary on a site lands on disk as .avif and then won't go into a slide deck, an older editor or an upload form.

Underneath, AVIF, the AV1 Image File Format, is HEIF: a structure of boxes that holds image items and their properties. Each picture is compressed with AV1, the royalty-free video codec the Alliance for Open Media released in 2018, and version 1.0.0 of the AVIF specification followed on 19 February 2019.

Transparency gets an item of its own. The alpha plane is coded as a separate auxiliary image tied to the main picture, which is how an AVIF logo or cut-out keeps soft, partly see-through edges. A file can also hold an image sequence, Exif, XMP and an ICC profile, at up to 12 bits per channel. Decoding all of this is slow, and an AVIF appears only once it is fully decoded instead of sharpening as it loads.

### Programs that open AVIF files

**Windows**

- Edge and Chrome: open an .avif dragged into a tab, with no add-ons.
- Photos: needs two Microsoft Store add-ons, the HEIF Image Extension and the AV1 Video Extension, before it shows AVIF.
- GIMP: reads and writes AVIF from release 2.10.22.

**Mac**

- Safari, Chrome and Firefox: view AVIF files.
- ImageMagick: turns an AVIF into a PNG with one Terminal command.

**Linux**

- GIMP and ImageMagick: open and convert AVIF.
- avifdec: libavif's own decoder, which can write a 16-bit PNG.

**Web**

- Current versions of every major browser: Chrome from 85, Firefox from 93, Safari from 16.1 and Edge from 121.

**Mobile**

- Android: AVIF decoding is built in from Android 12.
- iPhone and iPad: Safari shows AVIF on current iOS versions.

### AVIF and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .avif with image/avif; .png with image/png.
- **Compression**: AVIF codes each picture with AV1's still-image tools, with or without loss. PNG filters every row of pixels and packs it with DEFLATE, never losing anything.
- **Transparency**: both have a full alpha channel. AVIF keeps it as an auxiliary image beside the picture; PNG stores it with every pixel. This converter keeps it.
- **Bit depth**: AVIF reaches 12 bits per channel and PNG up to 16, but the PNG made here has 8 bits per channel, so HDR and extra depth don't survive.
- **File size**: for a photo, a PNG is often several times the size of the AVIF. For flat graphics the gap is smaller.
- **Animation**: an AVIF can be an image sequence; this page converts its first frame only.
- **Metadata**: AVIF can carry Exif, XMP and an ICC profile. None of them is copied into the PNG.
- **Support**: nearly every program opens PNG. AVIF needs a fairly recent browser, viewer or editor.

Choose PNG when you need transparency, crisp edges or a file you will edit and save again. For photos you only want to share, the [AVIF to JPG converter](/avif-to-jpg/) gives a much smaller file, and [AVIF to WebP](/avif-to-webp/) keeps transparency at a smaller size than PNG.

### Other ways to convert AVIF to PNG

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: GIMP 2.10.22 or newer opens the AVIF; then choose File > Export As, end the name with .png and click Export.
- **ImageMagick (command line)**: `magick input.avif output.png` writes the PNG in one step.
- **avifdec (command line)**: run `avifdec input.avif output.png`, adding `-d 8` or `-d 16` to choose 8 or 16 bits per channel. A 16-bit PNG keeps more of an HDR picture's depth than this page does. For an image sequence it decodes frame one unless `--index` asks for a different frame or for every frame.

### Problems with AVIF files

- **Windows shows a blank thumbnail or won't open the file**: add Microsoft's HEIF Image Extension and AV1 Video Extension from the Microsoft Store, or open the AVIF in a browser.
- **"This browser can't open AVIF files"**: there is no AVIF decoder in your browser. Updating usually fixes it, and any current Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari works.
- **The PNG is far bigger than expected**: a photo stored losslessly is heavy. Convert photos to JPG or WebP instead.
- **An animation became a still picture**: only the first frame is converted. Keep the AVIF, or use a tool that writes animated output.
- **Colors look duller than in the browser**: the PNG has 8 bits per channel and no color profile, so HDR and wide-color highlights are lost.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the file is damaged or isn't really an AVIF. Save it again from its source.

guide.title: About PNG to SVG
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

A PNG is a raster image: a grid of pixels, each with its own color. It is lossless, so every pixel comes back exactly as stored, and it can hold an alpha channel for smooth, partly transparent edges. PNG began as a patent-free replacement for GIF, and today it is the usual format for logos, icons, interface art and screenshots; a Mac's screenshots are PNG files unless you change the setting.

The grid is also PNG's limit. A PNG has a fixed number of pixels, so printing it larger, cutting it on a machine or blowing it up for a banner shows soft edges and blocky steps. That is why people go looking for an SVG: a vector file describes shapes instead of pixels and stays sharp at any size.

SVG is a W3C standard, written in XML, that became a Recommendation in 2001 for version 1.0 and in 2003 for 1.1. It can hold paths, shapes and text, and it can also hold ordinary pictures embedded inside it. Those two options are the heart of PNG to SVG, and they give very different files.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows**

- Photos and Paint: view and edit PNG.
- Inkscape: opens a PNG for tracing into vector paths.

**Mac**

- Preview: views and exports PNG.
- Adobe Illustrator: places a PNG and traces it with Image Trace.

**Linux**

- GIMP: edits PNG and can save a BMP copy for Potrace.
- Inkscape: the free tracing tool on every desktop system.
- Potrace: a command-line tracer for black-and-white artwork.

**Web**

- Every major browser displays PNG, and Figma imports it into designs.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: PNG images open in Photos or the Files app.
- Android: Google Photos and the gallery app.

Other tracers exist too, such as CorelDRAW's PowerTRACE and a range of online vectorizers, each with its own settings.

### PNG and SVG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .png with image/png; .svg with image/svg+xml.
- **What is stored**: PNG stores pixels. SVG stores drawing instructions as XML text, and can embed pixel images among them.
- **Scaling**: a PNG has one natural size. An SVG made of paths redraws sharply at any size; an SVG holding an embedded picture does not.
- **Editing**: PNG is edited pixel by pixel in programs like GIMP. Paths in an SVG can be reshaped and recolored in Inkscape, Illustrator or Figma, or even in a text editor.
- **Transparency**: both support it.
- **Use with machines**: cutting plotters, laser cutters and embroidery software follow paths, so they need a traced SVG.

What this page makes is an embedded SVG. It does not trace your picture. The file contains a single image element whose data is your picture as a PNG, written by your browser and stored as base64 text, at the PNG's own pixel width and height. Nothing is resized or reduced to fewer colors, and transparency is kept. The result opens wherever SVG is accepted, but it is still pixels inside, it blurs when enlarged, and it is about a third larger than the PNG data it holds.

A tracing program works the other way. Inkscape's Trace Bitmap, Illustrator's Image Trace and Potrace look for edges and areas of color and redraw them as paths. You get a true vector that scales and cuts cleanly, but it is a redrawing: fine detail, soft shading and photos rarely survive well, and simple, high-contrast artwork such as a logo or a line drawing traces best. If you start from a JPG, the [JPG to SVG converter](/jpg-to-svg/) embeds it the same way.

### Other ways to convert PNG to SVG

- **Inkscape (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: choose File > Import to bring in the PNG, select it, then choose Path > Trace Bitmap (Shift+Alt+B) and pick a mode such as Brightness cutoff. Tracing redraws the image as shapes rather than copying it, and works best on simple, high-contrast art.
- **Adobe Illustrator (Windows, Mac)**: choose File > Place to add the PNG, open Window > Image Trace, pick a preset, then save the result as SVG. The trace replaces the placed image, and a high-resolution picture takes longer to trace.
- **Potrace (command line)**: save a BMP copy of the PNG, then run `potrace -s input.bmp -o output.svg`. Potrace doesn't read PNG, and it traces in black and white at a cutoff set with `-k`, which is 0.5 unless you change it.

### Problems with PNG to SVG

- **The SVG still looks blurry when enlarged**: it holds the original pixels. Trace the PNG if you need clean edges at a larger size.
- **A cutting machine or embroidery program ignores the design**: there are no paths to follow. Trace it in Inkscape or Illustrator first.
- **The SVG is larger than the PNG**: base64 text adds about a third. If file size matters and an SVG isn't required, keep the PNG.
- **A trace has thousands of tiny shapes**: photos and soft shading trace poorly. Simplify the artwork, raise the contrast or reduce the colors before tracing.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the PNG couldn't be read, usually because it is corrupt. Save a fresh copy from its source.

guide.title: About PNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

PNG, Portable Network Graphics, is a lossless raster format created as a patent-free successor to GIF. It packs pixels with DEFLATE, the same compression ZIP files use, after a filtering step that predicts each pixel from its neighbors. When the guesses are good, as in flat colors and repeated patterns, the file is small.

PNG is flexible about color. A picture can be indexed, using a palette like a GIF, grayscale or full truecolor, with 1 to 16 bits per sample, and it can add an alpha channel so each pixel has its own level of transparency. The current specification also covers animated PNG, which programs that can't animate show as a still image.

That design explains when PNG is a poor fit. A camera photo is full of fine noise that no filter predicts well, so a lossless PNG of a photo is often several times the size of a JPG that looks the same. That is the usual reason to convert: a photo or a big screenshot saved as PNG, and an email, form or website that wants something lighter, or that accepts JPG only.

You meet PNG files every day. Screenshots on a Mac are PNG files by default, design apps export logos and icons as PNG, and many websites use it for graphics with transparent backgrounds.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows**

- Photos: views PNG, including screenshots.
- Paint: opens PNG and saves a copy as JPEG.
- GIMP: free editor that exports PNG to JPG with a quality slider.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens PNG and exports JPEG.
- Finder: Quick Actions convert a PNG without opening any app.

**Linux**

- GIMP: the usual desktop editor.
- ImageMagick: converts PNG files from the terminal, one or many.

**Web**

- Any browser: PNG and its transparency display everywhere.

**Mobile**

- iPhone and iPad: screenshots and saved images open in Photos and Files.
- Android: Google Photos and the gallery app.

### PNG and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .png with image/png; .jpg or .jpeg with image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: PNG is lossless. JPEG splits the picture into 8x8 blocks, describes each block as a mix of frequencies with a discrete cosine transform, and discards fine detail; typical settings make a picture 10 to 20 times smaller than its raw pixels.
- **Transparency**: PNG has full alpha. JPEG has none, so this converter fills transparent areas with a solid color, which your browser's JPEG encoder picks.
- **Color depth**: PNG goes up to 16 bits per sample. JPEG stores 8 bits per channel.
- **Best fit**: PNG for screenshots, text, logos and anything you will edit again. JPG for photos you want to share or upload.
- **Animation**: an animated PNG gives its first frame here.
- **Metadata**: none is carried into the JPG.

What this page writes: a JPEG at quality 0.85, with the same width and height as the PNG. Quality numbers aren't shared between programs, so 0.85 here may not match 85 in GIMP.

### Other ways to convert PNG to JPG

- **Preview (Mac)**: with the PNG open, choose File > Export, set Format to JPEG and click Save. Transparent areas are filled in, since JPEG has no transparency.
- **Finder Quick Actions (Mac)**: Control-click the PNG, choose Quick Actions > Convert Image, then choose JPEG and a size. On some macOS versions the command is under Quick Actions > More.
- **Adobe Photoshop (Windows, Mac)**: with the PNG open, choose File > Export > Export As, set the format to JPG, lower Quality if you want a smaller file, and click Export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux)**: choose File > Export As, type a name ending in .jpg and click Export. JPEG can't keep transparency.
- **Paint (Windows)**: open the PNG and save a copy, choosing JPEG as the file type.

### Problems with PNG files

- **The transparent background turned solid**: JPG has no transparency. Use the [PNG to WebP converter](/png-to-webp/) for a smaller file that keeps it.
- **Text in a screenshot looks smudged**: JPEG blurs sharp edges. Keep text-heavy images as PNG, or shrink them with the [PNG compressor](/compress-png/).
- **The JPG is bigger than the PNG**: simple graphics with few colors compress better as PNG. Keep the PNG.
- **An animation stopped moving**: JPG holds one picture, so only the first frame is converted.
- **Quality drops after more edits**: each JPEG save loses detail. Edit the PNG and convert once, at the end.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the file is damaged or isn't really a PNG. Re-save it from the app that created it.
